guides.title: 72-hour emergency kit
guides.tldr: Start with at least three days of safe water, ready-to-eat food, essential medicines, lighting and communication supplies. Include one gallon of water per person per day as a starting point, and account for pets, heat, medical needs and accessibility.

Personalize

Maintain the kit

guides.deck: Build a small support network with people you already trust: agree check-ins, practical tasks and boundaries before a crisis. Assign realistic tasks

Choose backups

Set boundaries

Review together

guides.title: Adult & child choking
guides.tldr: If someone cannot speak, breathe or cough effectively, call emergency services. For a responsive adult or child, give 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts, repeating until the blockage clears or they become unresponsive. Use chest thrusts when pregnant or when you cannot encircle the abdomen.
steps: Assess the cough
If the person can cough effectively, encourage coughing and watch closely.
Call for help
Send someone to call emergency services, or use speakerphone without delaying care.
Give back blows and thrusts
Lean them forward for 5 back blows between shoulder blades, then give 5 abdominal thrusts; follow dispatcher guidance.
If unresponsive
Lower them safely and start CPR as directed. Remove only a clearly visible object; never blindly sweep the mouth.

guides.title: Adult hands-only CPR
guides.tldr: If an adult suddenly collapses, is unresponsive and is not breathing normally or is only gasping, call emergency services, get an AED and start chest compressions. Push hard and fast in the center of the chest at 100–120 compressions per minute; follow dispatcher instructions.

Call and get an AED

Give compressions
Place both hands in the center of the chest; compress at least 2 inches, avoiding more than 2.4 inches, and allow full recoil.
Continue
Follow the AED prompts and dispatcher instructions until responders take over or normal signs of life return.

guides.title: Apartment & high-rise fire
guides.tldr: If fire is in your apartment, leave by a safe route and close doors behind you. Use stairs, not elevators. If smoke or heat blocks the exit, keep the door closed, call the local emergency number and give your exact building, floor and apartment location.
steps: Assess the exit
Do not open a hot door or enter a smoke-filled corridor. Follow the building’s verified fire plan and announcements when safe to do so.
Leave when the route is safe
Take keys if immediately reachable, close doors and use the stairs. Do not stop for belongings or return after leaving.
If trapped, keep smoke out
Close doors between you and smoke and seal gaps if possible without delaying the emergency call. Move to a room with a window and signal your location.
Give a precise location
Tell responders the building address, floor, apartment and access needs. Do not break windows or jump; conditions outside may worsen smoke entry.
guides.without_help: Choose the immediate lower-risk location based on heat and smoke; do not force a blocked stairwell because help is delayed. Make your location visible and keep communicating if possible. Improvised high-rise descent is not a safe substitute for an escape route.
guides.household: Plan for stairs, mobility limitations, children and pets before an incident. Learn the building’s refuge and evacuation procedures directly rather than assuming another building’s policy applies. Record access needs and a safe neighbor contact when that can be done privately.
guides.pack_now: Keep the action checklist and written contact details accessible. Use the equipment named in this guide only when available and appropriate. Assign someone to check access, batteries and expiry dates before an incident; retrieving a kit must not delay the immediate protective action.
guides.next: Meet at the household assembly point once outside and report missing people without reentering. Review the escape plan after every move or building change.
guides.watch: Smoke can spread through corridors and stairs. Never wedge fire doors open. Stay-put policies are building-specific and do not override immediate fire or smoke in your location.

guides.title: Armed conflict
guides.label: CIVILIAN SAFETY
guides.deck: A civilian plan for shelter, communication, displacement, and unexploded hazards.
guides.tldr: If fighting or explosions are nearby, move away from windows and exposed areas into the most protective intact space you can reach safely. Keep family members together, shoes and essential medicines close, and a plan for losing phone service. Do not cross active fighting for supplies or touch suspicious debris. Assistance and safe passage may be unavailable; judge movement against the danger of staying.
steps: Choose shelter before the next attack

Prefer a designated protective shelter if safely reachable. Otherwise use the most protective intact interior area available, away from glazing. Consider collapse, fire and flooding as well as blast exposure; no ordinary room guarantees safety.
Keep essentials beside you
Gather a battery light, footwear, safe water, medicines and written contacts without exposing yourself to retrieve them. Keep corridors and exits clear.
Make a family check-in plan
Choose nearby and out-of-area reunion contacts. Use short private messages with your location and status; do not publish live movements or other people’s locations.
Reassess before moving
Confirm a destination and route as recently as possible with independent trusted information. A claimed corridor or ceasefire is not proof of safe passage. Do not cross active fighting.
Avoid explosive debris
Leave unfamiliar objects, wires, fragments and abandoned munitions untouched. Warn people from a safe position and use verified demining or humanitarian channels when safe.
guides.next: Inventory water, food, medical supplies and power for the people with you. Arrange care tasks and check-ins with trusted neighbours where safe. Verify humanitarian assistance directly; do not assume government, embassy or aid transport will arrive.
guides.watch: A lull is not an all-clear. Fire, damaged structures, unexploded ordnance and interrupted utilities remain dangerous. Avoid confrontation with armed personnel; local protection risks determine whether contacting officials is safe.

guides.title: Avalanche
guides.tldr: Stay out of avalanche terrain when conditions are unsafe. Read the local avalanche forecast before travel and choose a safer route; rescue equipment does not make a dangerous slope safe. If someone is buried, call rescue and start companion rescue only where you can avoid another avalanche.

Consult the local avalanche center and get training before entering snow-covered backcountry.
Choose terrain deliberately
Avoid avalanche paths and slopes identified in the forecast; turn around when uncertain.
Carry and know rescue gear
Each person needs a transceiver, probe and shovel and practiced companion rescue skills.
If an avalanche occurs
Note the last seen location, call rescue and assess continuing danger before searching.

guides.title: Boil-water advisory
guides.tldr: Use bottled water or bring clear tap water to a rolling boil for 1 minute, then cool it; above 6,500 feet, boil for 3 minutes. Use approved water for drinking, cooking and brushing teeth. Follow the exact local notice. Boiling does not remove chemical contamination.

Prevent accidental use

Follow the all-clear

guides.title: Burns & scalds
guides.tldr: Stop contact with the heat source safely. Cool a thermal burn promptly with clean running water for 5-20 minutes while preventing whole-body chilling, then loosely cover it with a clean nonadherent dressing. Seek urgent help for deep, large, sensitive-area burns or breathing trouble.
steps: Stop the exposure
Move away from the heat safely. Do not touch an electrically injured person until the power source is safely isolated.
Cool the burned area
Use clean running water promptly for 5-20 minutes. Keep the rest of the person warm, especially children; stop whole-body chilling.
Remove tight items
Remove jewelry and tight items before swelling if they are not stuck. Do not pull away material adhering to the skin.
Cover and seek assessment
After cooling, loosely cover with a clean nonadherent dressing. Get prompt care for deep burns, burns larger than the person’s palm or those involving face, hands, feet or genitals.
guides.without_help: Use clean available water to cool the thermal burn while seeking assessment; keep the unburned body warm. Breathing difficulty or smoke around the mouth or nose requires urgent help. Do not turn lack of specialist access into a reason to apply household remedies.
guides.household: A child can cool too quickly during whole-body showers. One caregiver should watch temperature and breathing while another manages water and contact with care. Keep labels or exposure details when chemicals or electricity were involved, without carrying contaminated items into a clean area.

guides.title: Chest pain & suspected heart attack
guides.tldr: New chest pressure, squeezing or unexplained discomfort with shortness of breath, sweating, nausea or pain in the jaw, back or arm can be a heart attack. Stop activity, call the local emergency number and rest. Do not drive yourself.
steps: Stop and seek urgent care
Help the person rest in a comfortable position. Request emergency medical assistance and an AED if someone can bring one.
Stay nearby
Monitor breathing and responsiveness. Symptoms can be subtle or come and go; do not wait for a textbook pattern.
Use medicines carefully
Assist with the person’s own prescribed medication as directed. Ask a dispatcher or clinician about aspirin; avoid it if contraindicated, allergic, unable to swallow, or uncertain.
If they collapse
If unresponsive and not breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED promptly. A heart attack can lead to cardiac arrest.

guides.title: Child & infant CPR
guides.tldr: If a child or infant is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call the local emergency number, begin CPR and get an AED. Compressions plus breaths are important for children and infants. Follow dispatcher coaching and current hands-on training.
steps: Check quickly
Check responsiveness and normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Gasping is not normal breathing. Place on a firm, flat surface.
Call and get an AED

Use speakerphone or send someone. If alone without a reachable phone after an unwitnessed pediatric collapse, give about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to call and get an AED; follow dispatcher guidance.
Give compressions

For a single rescuer, give 30 compressions at 100-120 per minute, about one-third chest depth: about 2 inches in a child and 1.5 inches in an infant. Use one or two hands for a child; current AHA infant CPR uses one hand or two-thumb encircling hands.
Add 2 breaths and repeat

Open the airway and give 2 breaths, each about 1 second with visible chest rise. Use a neutral head position for infants. If unable or unwilling to give breaths, provide compressions rather than no CPR.
Use the AED
Follow device prompts and pediatric pad instructions. Pads must not touch; use front-and-back placement when needed. Continue until normal signs of life, takeover, exhaustion or an unsafe scene.

guides.household: Plan for two roles: caller/AED finder and rescuer. Rotate compressions with minimal interruption if another capable person is present. Keep the child’s age, collapse circumstances and known medical needs ready for handover; new birth resuscitation needs a different protocol.

Assume wires are live even when they are quiet or the neighbourhood has no power. Do not attempt a rescue by touching a person or object in contact with electricity. Contact the utility or emergency services from a safe place.

guides.title: Earthquake
guides.tldr: During shaking, Drop, Cover and Hold On. Protect your head and neck beneath a sturdy table if nearby; stay indoors rather than running outside. If near the coast, strong or long shaking may mean tsunami danger: move inland and uphill once shaking stops.
steps: Protect yourself now
Drop onto hands and knees and cover your head and neck. With a mobility device, lock wheels and protect your head.
Hold on
Stay under sturdy cover until shaking ends. Keep away from windows and objects that can fall.
If outdoors or driving
Move away from buildings and lines. Pull over safely clear of bridges, wires and trees and remain in the vehicle during shaking.
Check secondary hazards
Expect aftershocks; avoid damaged structures and check for fire, gas leaks and tsunami warnings.

Take normal food, safe water, medicines, waste supplies and a familiar blanket if readily available. Include pet water in the household total.

Use a tag and a recent photo, and check microchip contact details before emergencies. Keep veterinary records privately.

Tell reachable responders where an animal may be, but do not return to fire, floodwater or active danger yourself.

guides.title: Evacuation
guides.label: MOVEMENT
guides.deck: A departure is easier when the destination and route are already decided.
guides.tldr: Leave a threatened location while a safer route and destination are still available. Take people, pets, essential medicines, identification, shoes, water and phone power; do not delay for belongings. Confirm the route and a place to stay, tell a trusted contact, and avoid flooded, closed or actively dangerous roads. Do not wait for an order when immediate danger is evident. Radiation or airborne hazards may make sheltering safer than travel.
steps: Confirm the order
Check the official zone, deadline, route, shelter options, and whether the order includes your address.
Gather people first
Account for everyone and pets. Take required medication and medical supplies, documents, accessible equipment, keys, and a charged phone. Do not spend critical time packing extras.
Choose a destination
Go to a trusted contact or designated shelter outside the hazard area. Check pet rules, accessibility, and transport needs.
Leave and report safely
Use current official routes. Share your destination with an out-of-area contact, keep fuel in the vehicle if relevant, and do not return until authorities say it is safe.

guides.deck: Move away from windows and exposed areas into the most protective intact shelter you can reach safely. Stay clear of damaged buildings and unfamiliar debris. Use a designated protective shelter if it is safely reachable. Otherwise choose the most protective intact interior space available, away from glazing. Consider fire, collapse, flooding and escape access; a basement is not safe if these hazards are present.

Reassess the building
Smoke, fire, instability or flooding may require movement to a safer reachable place. Do not interpret a quiet period as proof that streets or unexploded objects are safe.
Keep debris untouched
Never handle suspicious fragments, wires, containers or munitions. Keep children and pets away. Do not approach to take a photograph.

guides.title: Extreme cold
guides.tldr: Get into a warm, dry place, replace wet clothing and add dry layers. Confusion, extreme drowsiness or loss of coordination can indicate hypothermia; call emergency services. Use safe heat and never bring grills or generators indoors.

Limit outdoor exposure and protect hands, feet, head and face.
Change wet clothing
Use dry layers and blankets; warm the body gently.
Find safe heat
Use approved heaters as directed, keep them away from combustibles and maintain CO alarms.
Arrange help
If heat fails, contact local warming shelters and help people with limited mobility relocate safely.

guides.tldr: Move to air conditioning or a designated cooling space, reduce exertion and drink water regularly unless your clinician restricts fluids. Confusion, collapse or seizures in heat can mean heat stroke: call emergency services and start rapid cooling.
steps: Find a cooler place
Use air conditioning, a public cooling center or another safe indoor location.
Reduce heat load
Rest, loosen unnecessary clothing and use cool wet cloths or a cool shower.
Check on others
Older adults, infants, outdoor workers and people with illness may need help. Never leave anyone or pets in a parked vehicle.
Recognize an emergency
For altered mental status or collapse, call emergency services and cool the person while waiting; do not give drinks to someone unable to swallow.

guides.tldr: Do not enter an unsafe flooded building. Check structural, electrical, gas and contamination hazards before cleanup. Keep children and vulnerable people away, use suitable protection and stop if the work exceeds what can be done safely.
steps: Confirm safe entry
Do not enter standing water near electrical equipment or a structurally damaged building. Qualified assessment may be needed before work begins.
Separate clean and dirty areas
Create a clean place for drinking water, first aid and rest outside the work area. Keep flood-contaminated shoes and tools away from household supplies.
Use suitable protection
Wear protective boots, gloves and eye protection. Mold cleanup may need a properly fitting NIOSH-approved N95 or better respirator; it does not protect against gases.
Dry and clean safely
When safe, remove contaminated porous materials that cannot be cleaned and dry affected areas promptly. Follow product labels; never mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners.

guides.title: Suspected opioid overdose
guides.tldr: Unresponsiveness with slow, abnormal or absent breathing may be an opioid overdose. Call the local emergency number, give naloxone according to the product instructions if available, and begin CPR with breaths if not breathing normally. Do not delay CPR or an AED for naloxone.
steps: Check scene and breathing
Avoid needles, powders and traffic hazards. Check responsiveness and normal breathing quickly; gasping or gurgling is not reassuring.
Request help and equipment
Send someone to call and bring naloxone and an AED when available. Share the exact location and breathing status.
Support breathing and circulation
If unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR with breaths if able and trained; use an AED promptly. Give compressions if breaths are not possible.
Use naloxone and observe
Follow the actual device instructions, including repeat dosing. Do not interrupt CPR to wait for a response. If normal breathing returns, place on their side as appropriate and keep monitoring.
guides.without_help: Give available naloxone and resuscitation promptly while a helper seeks care. Keep monitoring after improvement: opioids can outlast naloxone and breathing can worsen again. Stay until a capable person takes over or the scene becomes unsafe.
guides.household: Keep naloxone accessible wherever overdose risk exists and learn how the supplied product works. Share emergency roles without stigma; the immediate objective is breathing and medical care. Keep children and bystanders away from needles and unverified substances.
guides.pack_now: Keep the action checklist and written contact details accessible. Use the equipment named in this guide only when available and appropriate. guides.watch: Do not let the person “sleep it off,” put them in a cold shower or give food or drink. Naloxone is not a substitute for breathing support or urgent care.

guides.tldr: Sudden facial droop, arm weakness or speech trouble may be a stroke. Call the local emergency number immediately, note when symptoms began or the person was last well, and stay with them. Symptoms that disappear still need urgent medical evaluation.

Use FAST: Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to act. Sudden loss of balance, vision changes or severe headache can also matter.
Record the time
Write down symptom onset or the last time the person was known well. Do not delay seeking care while completing a checklist.
Protect breathing
Keep them comfortable. If not fully awake but breathing, place on their side when safe. Do not give food, drink or medication to someone with swallowing difficulty.
Watch responsiveness
If unresponsive and not breathing normally, begin CPR and use an AED. Follow dispatcher instructions when available.

guides.label: FIRE / AIR
guides.deck: Separate an approaching fire from a smoke exposure problem.
guides.tldr: For smoke without an immediate fire threat, stay indoors with windows and doors closed, use filtered recirculated air or a portable air cleaner, and check local air-quality updates. If ordered to evacuate, leave promptly. Severe breathing difficulty requires emergency medical help.
steps: Know which problem you face
Check official fire, evacuation, and air-quality notices for your address. An evacuation order changes the decision immediately.
If leaving, leave early
Take people, pets, medication, keys, and essentials; tell a contact where you are going. Use the evacuation guide and current route instructions.
If sheltering from smoke
Close windows and doors. Set HVAC to recirculate where possible, use a portable air cleaner or a cleaner indoor room, and avoid adding indoor smoke from candles, frying, or smoking.
Limit outside exposure
If you must go outside in smoke, a well-fitting N95 or P100 respirator can reduce particle exposure; ordinary cloth masks do not provide the same protection.

guides.title: Winter storm
guides.tldr: Stay indoors and postpone travel during dangerous snow, ice or blowing snow. Keep heat safe, use battery lighting and watch for power loss. If stranded in a vehicle, stay with it unless a safer shelter is clearly accessible.
